title: India Backs UN Equal Earth Map Resolution but Draws Red Line Over Kashmir Depiction
excerpt: The UN General Assembly adopted the 'Correct the Map' resolution by 164-1, with India voting in favour while insisting Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh be depicted per its official map.
body:
• The UN General Assembly adopted the "Correct the Map" resolution on September 4, 2026, by a vote of 164-1, with the United States the sole dissenter and six abstentions.
  • India voted in favour of promoting equal-area map projections but issued a firm warning that Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh must be depicted according to India's official map.
  • MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal clarified the resolution does not endorse any specific map, projection, or depiction of national boundaries.
  • The advisory resolution could influence school curricula, government publications, and digital mapping platforms if states choose to adopt equal-area projections.

India voted in favour of a United Nations General Assembly resolution promoting equal-area world maps on September 4 but simultaneously drew a sharp diplomatic line: any representation of Indian territory, including the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, must conform to India's official map.

What the Resolution Says

Titled "Correct the Map: Rebalancing Global Cartographic Representation and Promoting Equitable Representation of the World's Regions, Particularly Africa," the resolution was led by Togo and backed by the African Union. It passed by 164 votes to 1, with the United States casting the sole opposing vote and six countries abstaining.

The measure encourages the use of equal-area map projections — such as the Equal Earth projection — that preserve the true relative sizes of continental landmasses. Traditional maps based on the 16th-century Mercator projection distort size, making Greenland appear as large as Africa when it is, in reality, roughly one-fourteenth the size. Sponsors framed the push as correcting colonial-era cartographic bias that systematically shrinks equatorial regions.

The resolution is advisory and implementation is voluntary, meaning any actual change depends on action by governments, education systems, publishers, and digital mapping platforms.

India's Dual Position

Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said India's vote supported "the broader principle of using equal-area map projections" that preserve the relative sizes of continental landmasses. In an explanation of vote at the General Assembly, Indian diplomat Raghoo Puri emphasized that the resolution should be understood as promoting equal-area representation generally, not as endorsing the Equal Earth projection or any other specific system.

"India's sovereign territory, including the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, must be depicted in accordance with India's official map."

— Randhir Jaiswal, MEA spokesperson

Jaiswal stressed that the resolution "neither adopts nor authenticates any particular world map, nor does it address political cartography, including international boundaries, disputed territories or place names." India's position creates a deliberate distinction: it supports correcting geographic distortions but will not accept what it considers inaccurate political or territorial representation.

Why Maps Are Political

The controversy underscores why world maps are more than geographic illustrations. Map projections inevitably involve trade-offs — choosing an equal-area projection prioritizes accurate representation of landmass size, while political maps must additionally deal with boundaries, disputed territories, and national sovereignty claims. India has long taken a strict position on cartographic representation, with laws requiring the use of its official Survey of India maps and a history of objecting to foreign depictions that show Kashmir differently from New Delhi's position.

What Changes

Because the resolution is non-binding, near-term effects depend on whether governments and institutions act on it. The areas to watch include school curricula, government publications, default settings on platforms like Google Maps and Apple Maps, and the maps used in UN and multilateral communications. For India, the diplomatic maneuver combines alignment with the Global South's push against Eurocentric cartographic norms with a firm assertion of sovereignty — a balancing act that NRI families abroad may encounter as classroom maps and atlases potentially evolve.
